rows.verified: HSE electrical-safety guidance requires employers to assess electrical hazards and put suitable controls in place.
Work on electrical equipment should be thoroughly planned so the work and the completed installation are safe.
Equipment, machinery and installations should be isolated from electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic and other energy sources before work where applicable.
Energy isolation should be secure so energy cannot be inadvertently reintroduced.
People working on electrical equipment, machinery or installations must be competent for the task.
Competence should be supported by appropriate training, relevant experience and regular reassessment.
Electrical equipment must be maintained to prevent danger.
The type and frequency of checks, inspections and testing should reflect the equipment, its environment and previous results.
Electrical risk depends on voltage, current path, equipment condition, environment, task, isolation, protective devices and worker competence.
HSE electrical evidence is equipment-, installation-, task-, worker-, environment- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
HSE states that construction dust is a real risk to workers' lungs rather than merely a nuisance.
The COSHH Regulations require dutyholders to protect workers from hazardous construction dusts.
HSE recommends an Assess, Control and Review model for construction-dust risks.
Regular exposure to construction dust can contribute to lung cancer, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and silicosis.
Many common construction tasks can generate high dust levels.
HSE's CIS36 guidance is intended to help employers prevent or adequately control construction-dust exposure.
On-tool extraction can be used to control dust at source during relevant construction tasks.
Dust controls should be selected, used and maintained so that their effectiveness is sustained.
Construction-dust risk depends on material, silica content, task, duration, control method, extraction performance, respiratory protection and worker susceptibility.
HSE construction-dust evidence is task-, material-, workplace-, control-, worker- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level disease probability.
